cards.front: What is a Private Cloud?
cards.back: Cloud used by one organisation only. More control and security, but costlier.

cards.front: What is a Public Cloud?
cards.back: Shared cloud run by a provider (e.g. AWS). Cheap and scalable, but less control.

cards.front: What is a Hybrid Cloud?
cards.back: A mix: sensitive data on private cloud, everything else on cheaper public cloud.

cards.front: What does IaaS stand for and what does it provide?
cards.back: Infrastructure as a Service: rented servers, storage and networking; you manage the OS. E.g. Amazon EC2.

cards.front: What does SaaS stand for and what does it provide?
cards.back: Software as a Service: subscription software over the internet, e.g. Microsoft 365.

cards.front: What does PaaS stand for and what does it provide?
cards.back: Platform as a Service: build and deploy apps without managing servers, e.g. Heroku.

cards.front: Give TWO benefits and TWO drawbacks of cloud computing for an organisation.
cards.back: Benefits: lower upfront cost, scalable. Drawbacks: needs internet, data held by a third party.

cards.front: What is a VPN and how does it enable remote working?
cards.back: An encrypted tunnel to the company network, so remote staff work securely as if in the office.

cards.front: What is remote desktop technology?
cards.back: Viewing and controlling another computer remotely, e.g. TeamViewer for IT support.

cards.front: Why is security a factor when selecting an online system?
cards.back: Breaches bring fines and reputational damage, so providers must be GDPR-compliant and encrypt data.

cards.front: What is scalability in the context of cloud computing?
cards.back: Increasing or reducing resources on demand, e.g. scaling up for Christmas.

cards.front: Give TWO ways social media can be used by an organisation and ONE risk.
cards.back: Uses: marketing, customer service. Risk: negative comments spread fast.

cards.front: What is a wiki and what is its main limitation?
cards.back: A site anyone can edit (e.g. Wikipedia). Limitation: content may be inaccurate.

cards.front: Difference between a chatroom and a forum?
cards.back: Chatroom: real-time. Forum: posts stay up and people reply in their own time.

cards.front: What privacy consideration must organisations be aware of when using online communities?
cards.back: Users must consent to data collection (GDPR), so a clear privacy policy is needed.

cards.front: What is an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP)?
cards.back: Rules for how staff use IT and behave online, e.g. no sharing confidential data.

cards.front: What is a blog/vlog and give ONE organisational use?
cards.back: Regular written posts (blog) or videos (vlog). Use: showing expertise to engage customers.

cards.front: What is instant messaging and give ONE advantage over email for organisations?
cards.back: Real-time messaging, e.g. Teams. Advantage: faster replies than email.

cards.front: What is a podcast and give ONE use for an organisation?
cards.back: On-demand audio episodes. Use: staff training or marketing.

cards.front: State FOUR factors (other than security and scalability) that affect the selection of an online system.
cards.back: Cost, ease of use, features and connectivity.

cards.front: What is malware? Give THREE examples.
cards.back: Software designed to cause harm, e.g. viruses, ransomware, spyware.

cards.front: What is social engineering? Give an example.
cards.back: Tricking people into giving away information, e.g. phishing emails.

cards.front: State THREE impacts of a data breach on an organisation.
cards.back: Data loss, financial loss (GDPR fines) and reputational damage.

cards.front: What is encryption and how does it protect data?
cards.back: Scrambles data so only someone with the decryption key can read it.

cards.front: What is Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) and why is it more secure than a password alone?
cards.back: Two or more factors (know / have / are), so a stolen password alone isn't enough.

cards.front: What does a firewall do?
cards.back: Filters incoming and outgoing traffic using rules, blocking unauthorised access.

cards.front: What is unauthorised access (hacking)? Distinguish between a black-hat and white-hat hacker.
cards.back: Access without permission. Black-hat: malicious and illegal. White-hat: hired to test security.

cards.front: How can accidental damage threaten data? Give TWO examples and ONE protection method.
cards.back: Dropped laptops, spills, power surges. Protect with backups or a UPS.

cards.front: How do natural disasters threaten IT systems? How can organisations protect against this?
cards.back: Floods and fires can destroy on-site data. Protect with off-site or cloud backups.

cards.front: State FOUR internal threats to data within an organisation.
cards.back: Risky websites, accidental disclosure, staff leaking data, portable devices.

cards.front: What are file permissions and access levels? How do they protect data?
cards.back: Control who can read, write or run files, so users only access what they need.

cards.front: What is a backup? What should a good backup strategy include?
cards.back: A separate copy for restoring lost data. Use 3-2-1: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site.

cards.front: What are biometric security methods? Give TWO examples and ONE advantage over passwords.
cards.back: ID by body features, e.g. fingerprint, face. Advantage: can't be forgotten or shared.

cards.front: What is physical access control? Give THREE examples.
cards.back: Restricting physical entry, e.g. swipe cards, PIN-locked doors, CCTV.

cards.front: What is a digital certificate and how is it used?
cards.back: Proves a website's identity; issued by a Certificate Authority. Gives the HTTPS padlock.

cards.front: What does antivirus software do? State THREE key functions.
cards.back: Scans for known malware, protects in real time, and quarantines infected files.

cards.front: What is Wi-Fi and give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage?
cards.back: Wireless networking by radio. Advantage: no cables. Disadvantage: weaker through walls, less secure.

cards.front: What is Ethernet? Give ONE advantage over Wi-Fi.
cards.back: Wired networking by cable. Advantage: faster, more reliable and more secure.

cards.front: Describe a star network topology.
cards.back: Every device connects to a central switch. If the switch fails, everything goes down.

cards.front: What is a WAN and how does it differ from a LAN?
cards.back: A WAN covers a large area using third-party lines. A LAN covers one site you own.

cards.front: What is a VPN and why would an organisation use one?
cards.back: An encrypted tunnel over the internet, securely linking remote staff or branches.

cards.front: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
cards.back: HTTPS encrypts data with SSL/TLS; HTTP doesn't.

cards.front: What is bandwidth and what is latency?
cards.back: Bandwidth: data per second (Mbps). Latency: delay before data arrives (ms).

cards.front: Difference between lossy and lossless compression?
cards.back: Lossy permanently removes data (JPEG, MP3). Lossless keeps it all (ZIP, PNG).

cards.front: What is Bluetooth? Give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage.
cards.back: Short-range wireless (~10 m). Advantage: easy pairing. Disadvantage: short range, slower than Wi-Fi.

cards.front: What is USB? State TWO uses and ONE advantage over wireless connections.
cards.back: Wired data and power. Uses: peripherals, flash drives. Advantage: faster and more reliable than Bluetooth.

cards.front: Describe a ring network topology. Give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage.
cards.back: Devices in a loop, data flows one way. Advantage: copes with heavy load. Disadvantage: one failure breaks it.

cards.front: Describe a bus network topology. Give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage.
cards.back: All devices on one backbone cable. Advantage: cheap. Disadvantage: if the cable fails, everything fails.

cards.front: What is a Personal Area Network (PAN)? Give ONE example.
cards.back: A network of a few metres around one person, e.g. a phone linked to earbuds.

cards.front: What is the difference between SMTP, POP3, and IMAP?
cards.back: SMTP sends. POP3 downloads to one device. IMAP keeps mail synced across devices.

cards.front: What is VoIP? Give ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage.
cards.back: Voice calls over the internet. Advantage: cheap. Disadvantage: depends on connection quality.

cards.front: Why does file format matter when transmitting data? Give an example.
cards.back: It affects size, compatibility and quality, e.g. RAW images are far bigger than JPEGs.

cards.front: What is a codec and why is it needed for audio/video?
cards.back: Compresses and decompresses audio/video so it's small enough to stream, e.g. H.264.

cards.front: Give TWO benefits of online retail for customers and ONE risk.
cards.back: Benefits: shop 24/7, wider choice. Risk: payment data could be breached.

cards.front: What is targeted marketing? How does it use IT?
cards.back: Personalised adverts from browsing and purchase data, e.g. Amazon recommendations.

cards.front: What is verification in data entry?
cards.back: Checking data was entered correctly, e.g. double entry. It doesn't check the data is sensible.

cards.front: What is validation? Give TWO types.
cards.back: Automatic checks that data is sensible, e.g. range check, presence check.

cards.front: Give TWO benefits and TWO risks of online financial services for customers.
cards.back: Benefits: 24/7 access, instant transfers. Risks: phishing, data breaches.

cards.front: Give TWO benefits and ONE limitation of online education and training.
cards.back: Benefits: learn anywhere, often cheaper. Limitation: less face-to-face interaction.

cards.front: Give ONE advantage and TWO risks of accessing news and information online.
cards.back: Advantage: instant news. Risks: fake news and filter bubbles.

cards.front: Give TWO impacts of the growth of online entertainment on traditional businesses.
cards.back: Physical media sales have collapsed (e.g. HMV closures) and TV competes with streaming.

cards.front: What are online booking systems? Give TWO benefits and ONE risk.
cards.back: Online reservations, e.g. flights. Benefits: 24/7, lower admin costs. Risk: downtime stops bookings.

cards.front: What is transactional data and how do organisations use it?
cards.back: Data from purchases, clicks and logins. Used for recommendations, marketing and fraud detection.

cards.front: What is collaborative working using IT? Give TWO tools and ONE benefit.
cards.back: Working on shared files from anywhere. Tools: Microsoft 365, Zoom. Benefit: less travel.

cards.front: State THREE IT tools that enable remote working and ONE organisational implication.
cards.back: VPN, video calls, cloud storage. Implication: less office space needed, but higher security risk.

cards.front: What is the difference between primary and secondary data? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Primary: collected yourself (e.g. a questionnaire). Secondary: someone else's (e.g. census data).

cards.front: Give THREE methods of ensuring the reliability of information.
cards.back: Cross-reference sources, use credible sources, and check the date.

cards.front: Name FOUR methods of collecting data/opinions. Give ONE advantage of each.
cards.back: Survey: reaches many. Questionnaire: easy to compare. Focus group: in-depth. Interview: follow-ups.

cards.front: Give THREE reasons why data accuracy is important for organisations.
cards.back: Better decisions, GDPR compliance, and customer trust.

cards.front: Give THREE characteristics of a good user interface for a data collection system.
cards.back: Easy to use, accessible, and prevents errors (validation, drop-downs).

cards.front: What is virtual memory?
cards.back: Using part of the disk as extra RAM when RAM is full. Slower than real RAM.

cards.front: Name and describe FOUR types of user interface.
cards.back: CLI (typed commands), GUI (windows and icons), menu-driven (e.g. ATM), touchscreen.

cards.front: Difference between open source and proprietary software?
cards.back: Open source: free, editable code (Linux). Proprietary: closed code, usually paid (Windows).

cards.front: Give FOUR characteristics of storage media.
cards.back: Capacity, cost per GB, speed and compatibility.

cards.front: What is a personal computer (PC)? State ONE difference between a desktop and a laptop.
cards.back: A general-purpose computer for one user. Desktops are more powerful; laptops are portable.

cards.front: What is a multifunctional device (MFD)?
cards.back: One device that prints, scans and copies, saving space and cost.

cards.front: What are mobile devices? Give TWO advantages and ONE disadvantage for users.
cards.back: Phones and tablets. Advantages: portable, always connected. Disadvantage: easily lost or stolen.

cards.front: Name THREE types of server and state the function of each.
cards.back: File server: stores shared files. Application server: runs apps. Web server: serves web pages.

cards.front: What are entertainment systems? Give TWO examples and ONE impact of internet connectivity.
cards.back: E.g. consoles, smart TVs. The internet adds streaming and online multiplayer.

cards.front: What is the difference between a still digital camera and a video camera?
cards.back: A still camera takes photos; a video camera records footage.

cards.front: What are navigation systems? Give TWO examples of their use.
cards.back: GPS location and routing, e.g. sat navs and fleet tracking.

cards.front: What is an embedded system? Give TWO examples.
cards.back: A computer inside a device doing one job, e.g. a washing machine or car ECU.

cards.front: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)? Give TWO examples.
cards.back: Everyday objects connected to the internet, e.g. smart thermostats, fitness trackers.

cards.front: How are digital devices used in healthcare? Give TWO examples.
cards.back: Patient monitoring and electronic health records.

cards.front: How are digital devices used in manufacturing? Give TWO examples.
cards.back: CNC machines and robotic assembly arms.

cards.front: How are digital devices used in education? Give TWO examples.
cards.back: Interactive whiteboards and VLEs like Google Classroom.

cards.front: What is a flowchart? Name FOUR standard symbols used.
cards.back: A diagram of a process's steps. Oval (start/end), rectangle (process), diamond (decision), parallelogram (input/output).

cards.front: Name FOUR input devices and describe their use.
cards.back: Keyboard (typing), mouse (pointing), barcode scanner (stock), microphone (audio).

cards.front: Name FOUR output devices and describe their use.
cards.back: Monitor (display), printer (hard copy), speakers (audio), projector (presentations).

cards.front: Name FOUR assistive technologies and state who benefits from each.
cards.back: Screen reader (visually impaired), adaptive keyboard (motor), braille display (blind), eye tracking (severe motor).

cards.front: What is the difference between manual and automatic data processing?
cards.back: Manual: done by a person, slower and error-prone. Automatic: done by the system, fast and consistent.

cards.front: Name SIX types of operating system and briefly describe each.
cards.back: Batch (jobs in groups), multitasking, network, real-time (instant, e.g. aircraft), mobile, multi-user.

cards.front: How does the operating system manage networking?
cards.back: It handles protocols and connections, shares out network resources, and gets IPs via DHCP.

cards.front: How does the operating system manage security?
cards.back: Access control, antivirus, drive encryption, firewall and audit logs.

cards.front: How does an OS manage multitasking?
cards.back: Scheduling shares CPU time between programs, switching fast so they seem simultaneous.

cards.front: What is a device driver and why is it needed?
cards.back: Software that lets the OS talk to a hardware device, e.g. a printer.

cards.front: How does an OS manage user accounts?
cards.back: Authenticates users, stores profiles, and sets permissions (admin vs standard).

cards.front: What is the difference between utility software and application software? Give an example of each.
cards.back: Utility: maintains the system (antivirus). Application: user tasks (word processor).

cards.front: Give FOUR factors that affect the choice of operating system or application software.
cards.back: Cost, compatibility, security and features.

cards.front: Name TWO image file formats and state ONE characteristic of each.
cards.back: JPEG: lossy, for photos. PNG: lossless, supports transparency.

cards.front: Name TWO audio file formats and state ONE characteristic of each.
cards.back: MP3: lossy, small files. WAV: uncompressed, high quality.

cards.front: Name TWO video file formats and state ONE characteristic of each.
cards.back: MP4: lossy, works everywhere. MOV: Apple's format, high quality.

cards.front: Give FIVE factors that affect an organisation's choice of IT system.
cards.back: User needs, cost, compatibility, security and connectivity.

cards.front: How is IT used for stock control? Give ONE example.
cards.back: EPOS updates stock on each sale and reorders automatically when it runs low.

cards.front: How is IT used for data logging? Give ONE example.
cards.back: Sensors record readings automatically, e.g. temperature in cold storage.

cards.front: How is IT used for advertising? Give ONE example.
cards.back: Targeted ads based on browsing data, e.g. showing trainer ads after a trainer search.

cards.front: State THREE ways a new IT system can impact an organisation.
cards.back: Training costs, implementation costs, and changed working practices.

cards.front: Give TWO ways AI/emerging technology affects IT systems, and TWO implications for organisations.
cards.back: Effects: optimised resources, predictive maintenance. Implications: fewer jobs, faster data processing.

cards.front: What does the Computer Misuse Act 1990 cover?
cards.back: Unauthorised access, access with intent to commit further crime, and unauthorised modification.

cards.front: What are the key principles of the Data Protection Act 2018 / GDPR?
cards.back: Lawful, specific purpose, not excessive, accurate, not kept too long, secure.

cards.front: What is a privacy concern in the context of IT systems?
cards.back: People may not know what data is collected or if it's sold, so clear privacy policies are needed.

cards.front: What is meant by 'unequal access to information technology'?
cards.back: The digital divide: cost, disability, age or location stop some people using IT.

cards.front: What is meant by 'user experience' as a consideration when choosing an online community platform?
cards.back: Ease of use, performance, availability and accessibility.

cards.front: Why is 'meeting user needs' an important consideration when selecting an online community tool?
cards.back: If the platform doesn't fit users' tasks, they'll switch to unauthorised tools.

cards.front: Why is cost a consideration when an organisation adopts an online community or communication platform?
cards.back: Licences, setup, maintenance and training all add up.

cards.front: What security considerations apply when an organisation uses online communities or communication platforms?
cards.back: Data sits on third-party servers. Mitigate with MFA, access controls and clear policies.

cards.front: What is downtime and why is it a consideration when using online systems or communities?
cards.back: Time a system is unavailable, which stops work. Check the provider's SLA uptime.

cards.front: Why is training a consideration when introducing an online community platform?
cards.back: Untrained staff make mistakes or avoid the system, and training costs time and money.

cards.front: Why is integration with current systems a consideration when selecting an online platform?
cards.back: It must work with existing systems (e.g. email), or staff end up re-entering data.

cards.front: How can online community tools affect an organisation's productivity?
cards.back: Positive: faster decisions and collaboration. Negative: constant notifications distract.

cards.front: How does cloud computing specifically impact INDIVIDUALS (as opposed to organisations)?
cards.back: Benefits: access files anywhere, always up to date. Risks: privacy, needs internet.

cards.front: When would an organisation choose IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS? Give ONE use case for each.
cards.back: IaaS: custom servers (AWS). PaaS: building apps (App Engine). SaaS: everyday software (Microsoft 365).

cards.front: Describe TWO environmental impacts of IT systems.
cards.back: Data centres use huge amounts of energy, and e-waste contains toxic materials.

cards.front: Why is equal access to assistive technology an ethical concern?
cards.back: Without it, disabled people are shut out of work and education (Equality Act 2010).

cards.front: What is netiquette? Give FOUR examples of good online behaviour.
cards.back: Polite online behaviour: no ALL CAPS, be respectful, don't share others' data, cite sources.

cards.front: What does copyright legislation protect? How does it apply to digital content?
cards.back: Original work (software, music, images) from being copied. Using unlicensed software is illegal.

cards.front: What do Health and Safety / Display Screen Equipment (DSE) regulations require?
cards.back: Assessed workstations, regular screen breaks, good posture and lighting, free eye tests.

cards.front: What are communication devices? Give THREE examples.
cards.back: Devices that send and receive data, e.g. smartphones, routers, VoIP phones.

cards.front: What is a system diagram and what is it used for?
cards.back: A diagram of a system's components and connections, used to plan and explain it.

cards.front: Name FOUR types of storage device and give ONE characteristic of each.
cards.back: HDD: cheap, high capacity. SSD: fast, no moving parts. USB: portable. Optical: cheap to distribute.

cards.front: What is a LAN? Give TWO advantages for an organisation.
cards.back: A network within one building. Advantages: fast, and shares printers and files.

cards.front: Give FOUR factors that affect an organisation's choice of network.
cards.back: Cost, security, performance and scalability.

cards.front: How do network components affect performance? Give THREE examples.
cards.back: Switch speed, bandwidth, number of devices, and cable type (fibre is fastest).

cards.front: What is a secure payment system? How is transaction data protected?
cards.back: Card payments protected by HTTPS, PCI DSS rules and tokenisation.

cards.front: State THREE security risks when transmitting data and a protection for each.
cards.back: Interception → encryption. Public Wi-Fi snooping → VPN. Fake sites → digital certificates.

cards.front: What is an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) and why is it important ethically?
cards.back: Rules for using company IT. It protects people from misuse and sets clear expectations.
